narrative:
Your application was denied because the prediction estimated a 78% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. In practical terms, that is a high-risk signal: you were treated as much more likely than not to struggle at the bar, so admission was not offered.

The strongest reason was your third-year class standing. You were in the lowest decile by Year 3, while accepted students averaged around the sixth decile; this was the single most influential factor and it pushed the prediction toward failure. The second most important factor was your LSAT score of 26, well below the accepted-student average of about 37; this also pushed toward failure. Your undergraduate GPA of 2.10, compared with an accepted average of 3.23, was the third most important factor, but among these top factors it was the only one that leaned toward passing, though it was not enough to offset the other two. Your gender and race were not used in the prediction.

To improve a future application, focus on the areas that carried the most weight: raise your LSAT through structured preparation and a retake, and address your academic record through additional rigorous coursework or a post-baccalaureate program. Ask admissions whether conditional admission or an explanatory addendum is possible, and consider applying after demonstrating stronger academic readiness.
